title: Theory of Computation
description: Turing machines and their variants, the universal Turing machine, the Church–Turing thesis, Gödel's incompleteness theorems, decidability, reducibility, computational complexity and NP-completeness.

topics.title: Turing Machines
topics.summary: A Turing machine has an infinite tape, a head that reads, writes and moves both ways, and accept and reject states that take effect immediately; formally it is a 7-tuple. Variants such as multitape and nondeterministic machines and enumerators all recognise the same class of languages.
subtopics: Why study theory of computation; finite automata versus Turing machines
Chomsky hierarchy recap
Formal definition: the 7-tuple (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q0, qaccept, qreject)
Configurations and the yields relation
Recognisable (recursively enumerable) and decidable (recursive) languages
Examples: w#w and strings of 0s whose length is a power of 2
Variants: multitape, nondeterministic, enumerators

topics.title: Universal Turing Machine, Church–Turing Thesis and Gödel
topics.summary: A universal Turing machine takes another machine's description with its input and simulates it, and the Church–Turing thesis holds that every real-world computation can be done by a Turing machine. Gödel's incompleteness theorems showed that consistent systems containing arithmetic have unprovable true statements and cannot prove their own consistency.
subtopics: Universal Turing machine and how it differs from a Turing machine
Church–Turing thesis (λ-calculus and Turing machines, 1936)
Definition of algorithm and Hilbert's tenth problem
Gödel's first and second incompleteness theorems
Gödel numbering and arithmetizing metamathematics

topics.title: Decidability
topics.summary: A problem is decidable when some Turing machine always halts with the correct yes or no answer; acceptance, emptiness and equivalence for DFAs and membership for CFGs are decidable. Acceptance for Turing machines (ATM) is undecidable, proved with Cantor's diagonalization method.
subtopics: Decision problems, decidable, undecidable and semi-decidable languages
Recursive (REC) and recursively enumerable (RE) languages
Decidable problems for regular languages: ADFA, ANFA, AREX, EDFA, EQDFA
Decidable problems for context-free languages: ACFG; every CFL is decidable
Undecidability of ATM
Diagonalization, countable and uncountable sets

topics.title: Reducibility and Decidability of Logics
topics.summary: A reduction converts problem A into problem B so that a solution to B solves A; if A is undecidable and reduces to B, then B is undecidable, which proves the halting problem, ETM, ELBA and the Post Correspondence Problem undecidable. Logics differ in decidability, and non-monotonic logics can retract conclusions when new information arrives.
subtopics: Meaning of reducibility, with everyday examples
The halting problem HALTTM and ETM
Computation histories and linear bounded automata (ALBA decidable, ELBA undecidable)
The Post Correspondence Problem
Decidability of logics: propositional logic and truth tables
Non-monotonic logics: default logic and the Tweety example

topics.title: Computational Complexity and NP-Completeness
topics.summary: Computational complexity classifies problems by the time and space they need, with classes such as P, NP, PSPACE and EXPTIME and the open P versus NP question. A problem is NP-complete when it is in NP and every NP problem reduces to it in polynomial time; SAT was the first, by the Cook–Levin theorem.
subtopics: Time and space complexity; Big O
P, NP, NP-complete; PSPACE and EXPTIME
Open problems: P versus NP, circuit lower bounds, de-randomization, quantum complexity
NP-hard and NP-complete; Cook (1971) and the Cook–Levin theorem
SAT, 3SAT and polynomial-time reducibility (3SAT to CLIQUE)
